            • EP_SAVE ($00) - blow RAM file to Eprom in slot 3
            • EP_LOAD ($03) - read file from Eprom in slot 3 into RAM file
            • EP_REQ ($06) - Check for "oz" File Eprom or File Area in slot C
            • EP_Fetch ($09) - Copy saved/deleted file from File Area to RAM
            • EP_Find ($0C) - Find active File(name) in File Area in slot C
            • EP_DIR ($0F) - Fetch filename from Eprom in slot 3
            • EP_First ($12) - Return first file entry in File Area in slot C
            • EP_Prev ($15) - Return previous file entry in File Area
            • EP_Next ($18) - Return next file entry in File Area
            • EP_Last ($1B) - Return last file entry in File Area in slot C
            • EP_TotSp ($1E) - Return amount of used file space in slot C
            • EP_ActSp ($21) - Return active file space in slot C
            • EP_FreSp ($24) - Return free file space in slot C
            • EP_Count ($27) - Return number of files in File Area slot C
            • EP_Stat ($2A) - Return file entry status (active or deleted)
            • EP_Size ($2D) - Return file size of File Entry
            • EP_Name ($30) - Copy File entry name to buffer at (CDE)
            • EP_Image ($33) - Return pointer to start of file contents
            • EP_SvFl ($39) - Save RAM file to Flash or UV Eprom to slot C
            • EP_New ($36) - Return pointer to future new entry in File Area
            • EP_Delete ($3C) - Mark File Entry as deleted on Flash or UV Eprom
            • EP_Format ($3f) - Create File Area in slot C, on UV Eprom or Flash Card
            • EP_NewFile ($42) - Write RAM file to File Card in slot C
            • EP_WrBlk ($45), Write a block of bytes to UV Eprom in slot 3
            • EP_Fptr ($48), Get file pointer via offset into file entry image
            • EP_Empty ($4b) - Poll for empty file area in slot number C
            • EP_SvAs ($4e) - Stream opened RAM file to Flash or UV Eprom to slot C

Under the HoodEmulator InternalsZX Spectrum Next: how the sound is madeOne AY chip

One AY Chip: Tones, Noise and Envelopes

Sixteen registers. Write three numbers, and the chip plays a chord forever, with no further help from the CPU. The whole soundtrack of the ZX Spectrum 128K was made from three counters, a random-number generator and a staircase. So how can so little make music?

The AY chip is the sound of the 128K era and of most Spectrum music since: game soundtracks, demo music, the trackers musicians still write in today. It is a generator (the overview’s word): once your program has set it up, it plays by itself, and the CPU is free to run the game. That is the whole point. A beeper tune keeps the CPU busy for every single edge of the wave; an AY tune costs a few register writes a frame, and the game hardly notices that the band is playing. The Next has three of these chips. Here we take one of them apart; the next chapter, TurboSound, puts the three together.

Read The Big Picture: Four Sources, One Mixer first: it introduces the four kinds of source and the difference between a generator and a level writer. If square waves and DACs are new to you, the background chapter How a Computer Makes Sound explains them. And where the chip’s output goes next is the subject of The Mixer: One Sum, Three Outputs.

The road ahead

We start with the parts of one chip and the sixteen registers a program reaches them through, by way of the 128K’s two ports. Then we follow the sound from its sources: the clock that drives everything, a counter that turns a period into a square wave, and a shift register that makes noise. The mixer register decides what each channel plays, with one case that surprises almost everyone, and the volume table turns a volume into a level on a curve rather than a straight line. Then comes the envelope, a volume that moves by itself in sixteen shapes; if you read only one section, make it that one. After a look at the two chips the Next can pretend to be, the AY-3-8910 and the YM2149, we make some music: a chord, the classic effects, and a bass line played by the envelope itself. We end with how Klive does the same.

The chip is in YM2149 mode (the state after power-on) unless a section says otherwise. Its counters step 218,750 times a second. Levels are in the units of the Next’s mixer: one channel at full volume adds 255. The waveforms are captured from Klive’s emulated Next at 48,000 samples a second, from programs checked to do what the text says; they show Klive’s mix, where the AY chips count up from 0 as they do on the hardware.

The parts of one chip

The chip was designed by General Instrument as the AY-3-8910, a programmable sound generator, or PSG; Yamaha made a compatible chip, the YM2149. The 128K used the first. The Next builds both into its FPGA, and a register chooses which one each of its three chips behaves as (you meet it in AY or YM, further on).

Inside, one chip has a handful of parts, all driven by one clock:

  • Three tone generators, one per channel, each a counter that makes a square wave at a pitch your program sets.
  • One noise generator, a shift register that makes random bits, shared by the three channels.
  • The mixer register, which decides for each channel whether it gets its tone, the noise, both, or neither.
  • An amplitude per channel: a fixed volume, or the envelope, a volume that rises and falls by itself; one envelope generator is shared by the three channels.
  • A volume table, the chip’s DAC, which turns each channel’s 4- or 5-bit volume into a level.
  • Three outputs, channels A, B and C, each 0 to 255 units, which go to the mixer.

Here is something to notice: every one of these parts is a small counter or a register. None of them can make a curve. Everything the chip plays is built from on/off signals and steps of volume, and that is exactly why the AY sounds the way it does.

Sixteen registers behind two ports

The chip has 16 registers, R0 to R15, each 8 bits wide, though many use fewer:

Your program reaches them through two ports, the 128K’s own:

  1. It writes the register’s number to port $FFFD, the register select port. The value must have bits 7–5 clear: it is a register number, 0 to 31. Only 0 to 15 exist; a write to a register numbered 16 to 31 is ignored.
  2. It writes the value to port $BFFD, the data port. The selected register stays selected, so the program can write it again without selecting it again.
  3. It reads the selected register back from port $FFFD. (On the +3’s timing, port $BFFD reads the same.)

A value written to port $FFFD with bit 7 set is not a register number; the Next uses those values to choose between its three chips (the next chapter’s Three chips, two ports). Values with bits 7–5 anything else but 000 or the chip-select pattern select nothing.

After a reset, every register is 0 except R7, which is $FF: all tones and noise switched off. With every volume at 0, the chip sits in polite silence until your program sets it up.

R14 and R15 are not sound registers at all: they are the chip’s two 8-bit I/O ports, A and B. On the 128K, port A drove the serial connector. On the Next, nothing is connected to them. R7 bits 6 and 7 make each one an output (1) or an input (0); an input reads $FF, as if every pin were pulled up, and an output reads back the value last written.

The clock that drives everything

The chip runs from the Next’s 1.75 MHz PSG clock, the 28 MHz master clock divided by 16. Inside, the chip divides it by 8 again, so its counters step 218,750 times a second. Let’s call one of those steps a tick of the chip. Every pitch, every noise and every envelope in the rest of this chapter is counted in ticks.

A counter that makes a square wave

Each channel’s tone period is a 12-bit number: the low 8 bits in R0 (channel A), R2 (B) or R4 (C), the top 4 bits in R1, R3 or R5. The tone generator is a counter that counts ticks:

  1. At every tick, the counter goes up by one.
  2. When it has counted to the period (it has counted period ticks since it last started), it starts again from 0, and the channel’s square wave flips: high becomes low, or low becomes high.
  3. So each half of the square wave lasts period ticks, and a whole period lasts twice that.

Here is a period of 3, tick by tick:

The pitch is therefore

frequency = 218,750 ÷ (2 × period)

Let’s tune up. The A of 440 Hz needs a period of 218,750 ÷ 880 = 248.6, so 249, which plays 218,750 ÷ 498 = 439.3 Hz: as close as a whole number allows, and too little out of tune to hear. Captured from the machine:

The 12 bits give periods from 1 to 4,095, and so pitches from 218,750 ÷ 8,190 = 26.7 Hz, a low growl, up to 109,375 Hz, far above hearing. A period of 0 plays as 1. The steps between pitches are fine at the bottom of the range and coarse at the top: 249 and 250 are 1.8 Hz apart, but 10 and 11 are almost 1,000 Hz apart, so very high notes come out of tune.

The 128K’s AY ran from a clock of about 1.77 MHz instead of 1.75 MHz. The same period plays about 1.3 % lower on the Next, a quarter of a semitone: a 128K tune keeps its tune, just a little lower.

Noise from a shift register

The noise generator makes random bits with a 17-bit shift register:

  1. At every noise step, all 17 bits move one place towards bit 0, and the bit that falls out of bit 0 is lost.
  2. The new bit 16 is bit 0 exclusive-or bit 2, taken before the move. (If the register is all zeros, as it is after a reset, a 1 is fed in instead, so that it gets going.)
  3. Bit 0 is the noise signal: on or off, like a tone.

The bits it produces look random, though they are worked out exactly: the pattern repeats only after 114,681 steps. Each step changes the output with a chance of about one half. Randomness on a budget, and nobody can tell.

The noise period

The noise generator’s counter runs at half the tone generators’ rate, 109,375 steps a second, and the noise period in R6 bits 4–0 (1 to 31; 0 plays as 1) divides it once more: the register steps 109,375 ÷ period times a second. A small period gives a high, hissing noise; a large one a slower, rougher one, closer to a rumble:

Even at period 31, the pattern takes 114,681 ÷ 3,528 = 32.5 seconds to repeat, so no ear ever hears it come round. Keep in mind, though, that there is only one noise generator per chip: its period is the same for every channel that uses it.

Tone, noise, both or neither

R7, the mixer register, decides what each channel plays. Bits 0–2 switch the tones of A, B and C, bits 3–5 their noise, and both are active low: a 0 switches the source on. Each channel’s signal is

(tone, or tone switched off) and (noise, or noise switched off)

which gives four cases:

  • Tone only (tone bit 0, noise bit 1): the square wave.
  • Noise only (tone bit 1, noise bit 0): the noise.
  • Tone and noise (both 0): on only where the tone and the noise are on, so a noise that comes and goes at the tone’s pitch: a pitched hiss, used for drums and engines.
  • Neither (both 1): the signal is always on, so the channel plays its volume as a steady level.

Captured on channel A, with the same tone (period 109) and noise (period 8) each time:

Look at the last row. Uhm, a channel with everything switched off is not silent? Exactly, and it has two consequences that catch programmers out:

  • A channel is silenced by its volume, not by R7. Switching off a channel’s tone and noise does not make it silent: it makes it a steady level, which you hear as a click when it appears and disappears. The silent way is volume 0. Let me warn you: this catches almost everyone out once.
  • The steady level is a DAC. A program that switches off a channel’s tone and noise and then rewrites its volume many times a second plays a waveform through the volume table: that is how 128K programs played sampled drums and speech on the AY, before DAC sound cards.

R7 bits 6 and 7 are not sound: they set the direction of the I/O ports, as Sixteen registers behind two ports explains.

Sixteen volumes on a curve

Each channel’s amplitude register, R8 (A), R9 (B) or R10 (C), sets its loudness:

  • Bits 3–0: a fixed volume, 0 to 15. 0 is silent.
  • Bit 4: when it is 1, the channel ignores bits 3–0 and follows the envelope (the next section).

The volume is not the level. It goes through the chip’s volume table, which turns it into the level that reaches the mixer. The table is logarithmic: each step up multiplies the level by roughly the same factor. Why? Because your ear hears loudness as a ratio: doubling a level sounds like the same step up whether it goes from 32 to 64 or from 128 to 255. On a straight scale, the top volumes would sound almost alike, and the bottom ones would jump.

The YM2149 has a table of 32 entries, and a fixed volume v uses entry 2 × v + 1, every other entry. The AY-3-8910 has a table of 16, one per volume. They are not the same:

At volume 15, both give 255. Below it, the AY table is louder: volume 8 gives 40 in AY mode and 27 in YM mode, volume 1 gives 3 against 2. So a 128K tune that uses middle volumes for its accompaniment sounds more balanced in AY mode, the chip it was written for.

The envelope: a volume that moves

An envelope is a volume that moves by itself. A channel whose amplitude register has bit 4 set takes its volume from the chip’s one envelope generator, which steps up or down at a rate your program sets, in one of sixteen shapes.

The envelope period is a 16-bit number, R11 (the low byte) and R12 (the high byte). Like a tone counter, the envelope’s counter counts ticks, and every period ticks (0 plays as 1) the envelope takes one step. A ramp from silence to full volume, or back, is 32 steps, so it lasts

32 × period ÷ 218,750 seconds

from 146 µs at period 1 to 9.6 seconds at 65,535. A drum hit needs a few milliseconds; a slowly fading note a second or more. Plenty of room either way.

The sixteen envelope shapes

R13 bits 3–0 choose the shape, and each bit has a name:

  • ATT (attack, bit 2): 1, the envelope starts at the bottom and climbs; 0, it starts at the top and falls.
  • CONT (continue, bit 3): 0, after one ramp it drops to 0 and stays there, whatever the other two bits say.
  • HOLD (bit 0), with CONT set: after one ramp it stops and holds its level.
  • ALT (alternate, bit 1), with CONT set: the next ramp goes the other way. With HOLD, the envelope holds the level at the opposite end of where the ramp finished.

Let’s work through two shapes:

  • Shape 13, 1101 (CONT, ATT, HOLD): it starts at the bottom and climbs (ATT); at the top it stops (HOLD), and stays at full volume. The sound of a note that swells and then sustains.
  • Shape 14, 1110 (CONT, ATT, ALT): it climbs; at the top, CONT keeps it going and ALT turns it round, so it falls; at the bottom it turns again. A triangle, forever.

Here are all sixteen, captured from the machine with the same period:

With CONT clear, ALT and HOLD do nothing, so shapes 0–3 are all “fall once, then silence”, the same as shape 9, and shapes 4–7 are all “climb once, then silence”, the same as shape 15. Did you notice that the ramps curve instead of running straight? Every step goes through the logarithmic volume table, so the level grows by a factor at each step, which your ear hears as an even climb. Sixteen shapes, eight sounds:

  • Fall once and stay silent (0–3, 9), or climb once and fall silent (4–7, 15): a plucked or struck note.
  • Fall, again and again (8), or climb, again and again (12): a saw tooth.
  • Fall and climb (10), or climb and fall (14), forever: a triangle.
  • Fall once and jump to full volume (11), or climb once and stay there (13).

Writing R13 restarts the envelope, even with the value it already holds: it goes back to the start of its shape at once. That is how your program strikes a new note with the same shape: one write per note.

32 steps or 16

In YM2149 mode, the envelope’s 32 steps go through the 32-entry table, each one to its own level. In AY-3-8910 mode the table has 16 entries, so the envelope uses only its top four bits: each level lasts two steps. The ramp takes exactly as long, but it climbs in 16 coarser steps:

The YM’s ramp shows fewer than 32 distinct levels at its bottom, because its table’s lowest entries come in equal pairs (1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3): there are 29 different levels in all.

AY or YM

The Peripheral 2 Setting register, NextReg $06, bits 1–0, sets what all three of the Next’s chips are:

  • 00 (the power-on value): YM2149.
  • 01: AY-3-8910.
  • 10: the register list calls it “ZXN-8950”, but the chips look only at bit 0, so it behaves exactly as YM2149. There is no third kind of chip, however exotic the name sounds.
  • 11: holds all three chips in reset: silent, registers cleared, writes ignored, until the mode is changed again.

What your program can see change between the two modes:

  • The volume table (Sixteen volumes on a curve): AY mode is louder below volume 15.
  • The envelope’s resolution (32 steps or 16): 16 levels in AY mode, 32 in YM mode, over the same time.
  • The bits a register reads back. In YM mode, every register reads back all 8 bits as written. In AY mode, the bits a register does not use read as 0: R1, R3, R5 and R13 keep their low 4 bits, R6, R8, R9 and R10 their low 5 bits; the others read whole.
  • Registers 16 to 31, which do not exist: in YM mode they read $FF; in AY mode they read register number − 16, as if the top bit of the number were ignored. Writes to them are dropped in both modes.

So how does a program find out which chip it is on? It writes a value with the top bits set to R1, say, and reads it back: whole in YM mode, its low 4 bits in AY mode.

One more read is the Next’s own: port $BFF5 (an address that the data port $BFFD also answers) reads the selected chip’s identity in bits 7–6 and the selected register’s number in bits 4–0, for software that must know which chip and register it last selected (the next chapter’s Three chips, two ports).

Playing a chord

Three channels, three notes. C, E and G above middle C are periods 209, 166 and 140 (523.3, 658.9 and 781.3 Hz). Set once, they play until something changes them:

A music player does not touch the chip while a note sounds. Once a frame, 50 times a second, it moves on in the tune: when a note ends, it writes the next note’s period and volume, or restarts the envelope with R13. A few register writes per frame is the whole cost of the music to the CPU. Not a bad deal for a band.

Effects, one register at a time

The once-a-frame player is also how the classic effects are made, by changing a register a little every frame:

  • Vibrato: the period moves up and down by one or two around the note, a wobble in pitch.
  • Tremolo: the volume moves up and down, a wobble in loudness.
  • Arpeggio: one channel cycles through the notes of a chord, a new one every frame or two, so a single voice sounds like a chord. Three channels can then play six or nine “notes”, the chip-music sound.
  • Slides: the period changes by a fixed amount every frame, for pitch bends and laser sounds.

Bass from the envelope

The envelope does not have to be slow. With a short period, a repeating shape is itself a waveform. Shape 8, a falling saw tooth, repeats every 32 steps, so with a period of 14 it plays 218,750 ÷ (32 × 14) = 488.3 Hz. Shape 10, a triangle, takes 64 steps for one cycle, so a period of 7 gives the same pitch:

These waves sound very different from the square tones, and much richer, which made the “buzzer” bass a favourite of AY musicians. The price is that there is only one envelope per chip: a channel that plays the bass takes the envelope away from the other two. Musicians often switch on the channel’s tone as well, at a pitch related to the envelope’s: the mixer register then lets the envelope’s wave through only while the tone is high, which gives yet another colour. I think it is one of the cleverest tricks ever played on this chip.

How Klive does it

Klive’s Next core is a C program compiled to WebAssembly; its three AY chips are one module, written to follow the hardware step for step.

Each chip keeps the same state as the hardware: its sixteen registers, its three tone counters and their outputs, the noise generator’s counter and shift register, and the envelope’s counter, level and direction. One tick of the emulated chip is one tick of the real one, every 128 master clocks. The chip is not ticked in step with the CPU, though: it is brought up to date when something needs it, a write to one of its ports or the moment a sample of sound is due, by running all the ticks that have passed since the last time.

The chip’s outputs change at its ticks, 218,750 times a second, far more often than a sample is taken. For the audio jack and the speaker, Klive averages each channel’s level over the time a sample covers, as the smoothing after the real converter would; for HDMI it takes the level at the sample’s moment, as HDMI does. The levels go to the mixer as the hardware’s are, from 0 upwards: unlike the beeper, Klive does not remove the AY’s constant level (the mixer chapter’s How Klive does it explains why). And if you want to read the code yourself, here is where it lives:

WhatWhere
The three chips: registers, ports, counters, noise, envelope, volume tables, AY and YM modessrc/emu/machines/zxNext/wasm/zxnext/zxnext-psg.c
Ports $FFFD, $BFFD and $BFF5zxnext-ports.c in the same folder
Where the outputs are addedzxnext-audio-mixer.c in the same folder

What to take home

Let’s take stock. One AY chip has three tone generators, one noise generator, a mixer register, a fixed volume or the envelope for each channel, and a logarithmic volume table. Out come three outputs, A, B and C, each 0 to 255 units. Your program reaches its 16 registers through port $FFFD, which selects one (bits 7–5 clear), and port $BFFD, which writes it; reads come from port $FFFD. After a reset, every register is 0 except R7, which is $FF.

Everything counts in ticks, 218,750 a second (1.75 MHz ÷ 8). A tone’s 12-bit period plays 218,750 ÷ (2 × period), so 249 is A at 439.3 Hz, and a period of 0 plays as 1. Noise comes from a 17-bit shift register fed with bit 0 exclusive-or bit 2, stepping 109,375 ÷ period times a second, with the period in R6, 1 to 31. R7 switches each channel’s tone and noise, active low, and a channel with neither plays its volume as a steady level: silence is volume 0, not R7.

R8 to R10 hold a fixed volume, 0 to 15 (YM entry 2v + 1, or the AY’s own table, louder below 15), or set bit 4 to follow the envelope. The envelope takes a step every period ticks (R11 and R12, 16 bits), 32 steps a ramp, and R13 picks one of 16 shapes from CONT, ATT, ALT and HOLD, eight of them different; every write to R13 restarts it. NextReg $06 bits 1–0 make the chips YM2149 (00 or 10), AY-3-8910 (01, with a 16-level envelope and masked reads), or hold them all in reset (11).

A few writes per frame play three voices; vibrato, tremolo and arpeggios rewrite registers frame by frame; and a short envelope period turns the envelope into a saw-tooth or triangle bass. Klive ticks each chip as the hardware does, brings it up to date whenever a port or a sample needs it, and averages each sample’s level. Three counters, a random-number generator and a staircase, and the rest, as they say, is music.
